turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Jacobs. Sleeve up for me, please, I'll do your observations before the doctor comes in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, okay. Can we not drag it out? I've been in that waiting room since seven and I'm finished.

[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, pulse eighty-eight, temperature thirty-six point eight. Oxygen sat is ninety-seven percent and you're breathing at eighteen a minute. Those are all fine on my side.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): They don't feel fine. This cough is doing my head in.

[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): I'll put the cough on the note. Your brother, when he dropped you off, mentioned a cousin who'd been ill, quite a long cough, and the family was worried it was TB. He wasn't sure it had been confirmed.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, please. My brother loves a story. I have not been near anyone with TB, and I haven't travelled anywhere. He can keep his opinions.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Howzit, Mr Jacobs, I'm Doctor Naidoo. Come, sit. Tell me what's been going on, in your own words.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the cough. Started with that flu and then it just stayed.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): The flu. How long has the cough actually been with you?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about six weeks. Well, actually, the flu was six weeks ago, and the cough has been the whole six weeks. It maybe started a few days into the flu, and I can't give you the exact day.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): And through the day, how's it behaving?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse at night. I lie down and off it goes. Daytime it's there, but not so hectic, and I'm hardly sleeping, which is why I'm so ratty, sorry.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't apologise, shame. Was there fever, or was that only with the flu?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Fever was with the flu, and that's gone. The aches as well. I'm not hot now.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you bringing anything up, any phlegm?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I can't honestly say.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that one, then. Any blood?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about getting short of breath, or pain in the chest?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I get a bit puffed on the stairs at work, but that's not new. The cough is what I came for.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): And your weight, any loss that you've noticed?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No weight loss.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eating all right through all of this?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, I eat. Though, well, actually, my trousers are loose, I had to take the belt in two holes. They're hanging off me, and I didn't clock that as losing weight.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): That counts, thank you for saying it. Any drenching night sweats?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I wake up coughing, not sweating.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been away recently, or around someone with tuberculosis?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I told Sister already. No travel. No TB contact. Work and home, that's my life.

[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, can I just come in. His brother was quite definite in the passage about a cousin in Polokwane, coughing for months, and the aunt thinks it was TB. Not confirmed, from what he said.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't buy that. I haven't seen that cousin in years, and my brother wasn't even there, he's just repeating my aunt's phone call. There was no contact.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. You don't recall any contact, and what reached me is second-hand and not confirmed. I'll note both, but I won't build a story on it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. Can we get on with it? I've got a shift later, some bakkie has blocked the parking, and I'm already irritated.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll keep it moving. What do you do on that shift?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Warehouse, packing orders. It gets dusty. Nothing like the mines.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Not hectic, about eight or ten a day. I keep saying I'll stop.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you taking anything for this cough, or any other medicine?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): A brown bottle from the chemist, some cough mixture. I take, um, two spoons at night, I think it's two. I never read the name on it.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): So we don't actually know the name, and the two spoons is a guess. Did anyone give you an antibiotic?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): The clinic did. Pink and white capsules, amoxicillin, five hundred milligrams, three times a day, for five days. I finished the lot about two weeks back, and the cough didn't care.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Finished, so that's stopped. Any regular tablets, for blood pressure or sugar or anything?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not a tablet person. Nothing else.

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to your chest. Big breath in, and out, and again. Your throat isn't red, the glands in your neck aren't up, and the chest is clear, no wheeze and no crackles.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's nothing serious, then. Can I go?

[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't call it nothing. Six weeks of cough, worse at night, and your clothes getting loose, that deserves a proper look. Folks will say post-viral cough, or a touch of asthma, or a lingering infection, or even TB, but I'm not naming a cause today, and I don't want to conclude any of those yet.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Then what am I supposed to do, just cough?
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): No. I'm sending you for a chest X-ray today, and the form goes in now. Let's see what the X-ray shows before anyone decides.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): And after that? I've got a shift, I can't keep coming back.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll book you back here next week to go through the result. Radiology is just down the passage, so you can do the film before you leave.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Next week. What if I get worse before that?

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): If your breathing gets tight, or you cough up any blood, or you feel properly unwell, don't wait for the appointment. Come back or go to casualty. Otherwise it's next week, and that visit is already booked.
[SEG0052] person_1 (NURSE): Come, I'll walk you as far as the passage. Radiology is the second door on the left.

features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

omissions.text: Possible sputum/phlegm production was discussed but left uncertain: the patient said 'Sometimes, not really. I can't honestly say,' so this symptom is indeterminate rather than absent or clearly present.
The patient denied current fever, saying he is 'not hot now.'

The patient denied noticing weight loss at first ('No. No weight loss') before later reporting loose trousers and belt tightened by two holes; this initial denial and subsequent clarification are not captured as a contradiction/change in history.
Eating/appetite was specifically asked about and the patient said he is eating ('Ja, I eat').
The completed amoxicillin course ended about two weeks ago.

The doctor documented diagnostic uncertainty/differential considerations: post-viral cough, possible asthma, lingering infection, or even TB, but explicitly said he was not naming a cause yet and did not want to conclude any of these today.
The chest X-ray was to be done today before the patient left, with radiology down the passage.
The doctor said the next-week follow-up visit was already booked and was specifically to review the chest X-ray result.
